scqa.name: SCQA (Situation–Complication–Question–Answer)
scqa.summary: Barbara Minto's pyramid-principle arc: surface the recommendation up front, then layer key arguments and supporting evidence beneath it. The default for executive memos, strategic recommendations, and consulting decks where the audience needs the answer fast.

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Establish the shared context: what is true today that the audience already agrees on. State only facts the audience accepts without argument. The goal is alignment, not persuasion — you are setting the stage.

beats.name: Complication
beats.description: Introduce the disturbance to the situation: what changed, what is at risk, what is no longer working. This is the tension that makes the audience lean in. Be specific and quantify the change where possible.

beats.name: Key Question
beats.description: Surface the question the complication forces the audience to answer. Frame it explicitly — 'Should we…?', 'How do we…?', 'What changes if…?'. The question should feel inevitable given the complication.

beats.name: Answer
beats.description: Deliver the recommendation in a single sentence, up front. No arguments yet, no caveats — just the conclusion the rest of the deck will defend. This is the apex of the Minto pyramid; everything that follows supports it.

beats.name: Key Arguments
beats.description: Lay out the two or three top-level reasons the answer is correct. One slide per argument, or one summary slide naming all of them. Each argument should stand alone as a compelling reason; together they should be exhaustive of the case.

beats.name: Supporting Evidence
beats.description: Present the data, examples, and case studies that ground each argument. Pyramid-principle style: every claim above is backed by something verifiable here. Cite sources; show the numbers; let the evidence carry the weight.

academic.name: Academic
academic.summary: Researchers, professors, and students expecting rigorous methodology, citations, and evidence-based conclusions.
academic.description: Researchers, professors, and students who expect rigorous methodology, citations, and evidence-based conclusions. Cite every source, show confidence intervals, be transparent about method, and leave marketing language out. Chart density can be high; 20-50 slides with time reserved for questions.

customer.name: Customer
customer.summary: End customers receiving product demos, onboarding presentations, or business reviews.
customer.description: Customers receiving product demos, onboarding, or business reviews. Speak in their language, focus on the value they realize, keep visuals simple, and use strong product screenshots. Keep chart density low; 10-20 slides.

pitch.name: Pitch
pitch.summary: Present an opportunity and ask for investment, approval, partnership, or sponsorship.
pitch.description: Use when the deck needs to create interest and move a high-stakes audience toward backing the opportunity. Lead with the opportunity, prove credibility, and make the ask concrete.
pitch.outcome: The audience agrees to invest, sponsor, approve, or continue the conversation.
successCriteria: Ask and next step are explicit

inspirational.name: Inspirational
inspirational.summary: Aspirational, narrative-driven voice for keynotes, founders, and rallying cries.
inspirational.description: Reach for shared belief and possibility, then ground it in something concrete. Use vivid imagery and rhythm; avoid collapsing into hype by always pairing aspiration with a real anchor.
voiceCues: Open with belief; close with action.
Use rhythm — paired phrases, repetition, deliberate beats.
Pair every aspirational claim with a concrete proof point.
Speak in present tense to make the future feel inevitable.
avoid: Stacked superlatives ('the very best, world-changing, revolutionary').
Dense data tables — push numbers into supporting slides.
samplePhrases: We're building the runtime that makes agents feel instant.
When latency disappears, what becomes possible?
The next decade of software belongs to teams who treat speed as a feature.

cover.name: Cover
cover.summary: The opening slide: title, subtitle and an optional picture.
cover.description: Open a presentation with its subject and a short introduction. Add a picture when it helps establish the context.

text.name: Text
text.summary: Prose. Several blocks sit side by side when short and stack when long.
text.description: Explain one idea in continuous prose. Use paragraphs or flowing blocks for detail that needs to be read in sequence.

chart.name: Chart
chart.summary: One to six charts, with an optional note.
chart.description: Give a chart enough space to show its evidence. Use the title to state the conclusion and labels to explain the measures.

table-beside.name: Table beside
table-beside.summary: A table with commentary beside it.
table-beside.description: Place a table beside its interpretation. Use the supporting text to explain the conclusion without repeating every cell.

timeline.name: Timeline
timeline.summary: Dated events or a roadmap along one axis, with optional notes.
timeline.description: Show events or milestones in chronological order. Label each item with a date or stage and a concise description.

list.name: List
list.summary: Bulleted or numbered points; one long list flows into columns.
list.description: Present several related points in a clear sequence. Use bullets for independent points or numbered items for an ordered list.
